classifiedFindings.label: M-01
classifiedFindings.title: setYieldStrategy sweeps unmatched idle balance into the strategy, making terminal migration unavailable until an undocumented cross-repo owner call -- REALIZED on two funded mainnet pools

classification.assetImpact: No direct asset loss and no theft path. The impact is the permanent loss of the protocol's ORDERED, LOSS-SOCIALIZING exit for the affected pool. initiateMigration -> batchMigrate/userMigrate pays every user the uniform snapshot credit p_i*min(R,P)/P; that path is the protocol's own designed remedy for an impaired strategy. Once bricked, an underwater strategy leaves withdraw blocked by the story-008 underwater guard and initiateMigration reverting, so the ONLY remaining exit is emergencyWithdraw, which this ledger already records (entry 0dca43f315) as realizing loss first-come-first-served. The defect therefore converts a proportional, order-independent haircut into a bank run: early exiters are made whole at the expense of late ones. That is a value REDISTRIBUTION under a stated assumption, plus a permanent loss of protocol function.
attackPath: 1. NO ATTACKER REQUIRED. The protocol's own documented revival runbook (initiateMigration -> batchMigrate -> finalizeAndReset -> setYieldStrategy) leaves floor-division migration dust in the staker's raw token balance that totalStaked does not account for. 62 wei observed over 21 revivals in the Tier-3 campaign.
2. Owner calls setYieldStrategy on the now-empty, revived pool. The story-010 gate require(totalStaked == 0) passes and PINS totalStaked at zero.

3. The sweep at :271-274 is bounded by IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) -- the RAW balance, not totalStaked -- so the unaccounted dust is deposited into the new strategy with NO matching totalStaked increment. The desync is now baked in and structurally permanent.
4. Users stake; the pool operates normally (stake/withdraw/claim all fine), so nothing surfaces.

5. Later, the owner calls initiateMigration. P = totalStaked, _routeExit withdraws exactly P, and the post-check require(strategy.principalOf(token, address(this)) == 0, "StableStaker: incomplete exit") sees the residual dust and reverts. It will revert on every future call.
6. If the strategy subsequently goes underwater, withdraw is blocked and initiateMigration is bricked -- only FCFS emergencyWithdraw remains.
classification.alternateTrigger: Permissionless: any address front-runs the owner's setYieldStrategy tx with a 1-wei token transfer to the staker. Cost is gas. Verified by test_oneWeiDonation_bricksTerminalMigrationForever.
classification.likelihood: high that the precondition arises (the protocol's own runbook produces the dust with no adversary and no misconfiguration); moderate that the consequence is realized (requires the owner to later need a terminal migration -- which is precisely the scenario the protocol explicitly anticipates and has built machinery for). The brick itself is CERTAIN and PERMANENT once step 3 executes.
classification.assumptions: The loss-redistribution leg assumes the strategy later goes underwater. The pure loss-of-function leg assumes only that a future terminal migration is ever wanted, which the existence of initiateMigration/finalizeAndReset presupposes.
classification.externalRequirements: None for the brick. For the FCFS-loss consequence: an impaired external yield strategy.
classification.remediationReach: Once the revived pool holds staked principal the brick is unfixable in place: setYieldStrategy requires both Active state and totalStaked == 0, so the strategy cannot be unwired while users are in it, and initiateMigration -- the only path to empty the pool -- is the very thing that reverts. Recovery requires every user to withdraw voluntarily first. There is no privileged clear.

classifiedFindings.justification: This is a textbook C4 Medium on both prongs of the definition. Assets are not at direct risk and no attacker profits, so High is not available -- I explicitly decline to inflate it. But 'the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted' is met squarely and permanently: a first-class, documented protocol function (terminal migration) is destroyed for the affected pool by an ordinary operational sequence, with no privileged remedy once users have staked. The second prong is also met independently -- there is a value leak with stated assumptions and an external requirement (an underwater strategy), where the leak is the difference between the designed proportional socialization and the FCFS realization that emergencyWithdraw imposes. Aggravating and decisive against any downgrade: the trigger is the protocol's OWN runbook rather than an error, the PoC reproduces against the real ERC4626YieldStrategy, and the brick is created by the story-010 empty-pool gate that was introduced as the FIX for three currently-acknowledged Mediums -- the remedy manufactures the defect. Aggravating for scope: the 1-wei donation variant makes it permissionlessly triggerable by anyone watching the mempool.
classifiedFindings.overstatementCheck: NOT overstated. I tested the downgrade case (no value loss, pool keeps working) and it fails, because C4 Medium does not require value loss -- availability and protocol function are sufficient, and here they are permanently destroyed with no admin clear.

classifiedFindings.label: L-06
classifiedFindings.title: initiateMigration is an unvalidated one-way door; the constructor omits _oldStaker != _newStaker, making a self-aliased migrator constructible

arbitration.SUPERSEDED: This block is RETAINED VERBATIM FOR THE RECORD and is NO LONGER OPERATIVE. Its conclusion (Medium UPHELD, code-scanner UNDERSTATING) was REVERSED on 2026-08-27 -- see `severityReversal` above. Its load-bearing factual premise ('no owner action unwinds this') is FALSE: StableStaker.setMigrator (src/StableStaker.sol:200) is an ungated owner setter. Do not cite this block as authority.
arbitration.disputeResolved: Argument A (pattern-matcher, Medium Law-3 footgun) is UPHELD; argument B (code-scanner, QA) is CREDITED as narrowing the reach but does NOT defeat the finding. This is not an average of the two positions -- it is A, with B's evidence used to scope which leg carries the severity.
whyArgumentBDoesNotWin: B's recovery PoC is real, passing and correct, and I re-ran it (4/4). But it establishes RECOVERABILITY, not harmlessness, and recoverability is not the Law-3 test. The Law-3 test is SURPRISE.

B's 'prominently documented, therefore obvious-leaning' claim does not survive reading the NatSpec. Section (C) documents a REQUIREMENT ('two-sided wiring is required before use'); it nowhere documents that violating that requirement is only DETECTABLE after the irreversible step has already fired, and it nowhere documents that a self-aliased migrator is constructible. Documenting a precondition is not documenting the failure mode of omitting it. Per project law, a reassuring or falsely-exhaustive doc block carries no suppression authority.

B's own PoC contains the refutation. Three of its four tests show clean recovery; the fourth, test_same_staker_constructor_is_inert_but_still_burns_the_pool, shows the aliasing case where the ONLY remedy is every user self-exiting by hand and the owner cannot clear it at all. B wrote the counter-example to its own conclusion.
B is therefore recorded as UNDERSTATING this finding.
arbitration.law3SurpriseTest: Would a competent, non-malicious owner be surprised? YES, on two counts. (1) The contract's own NatSpec section (C) declares three destination preconditions mandatory -- token registered via addToken, migrator wired via setMigrator, destination authorized as a phUSD minter -- and NOTHING checks any of them, yet the forwarded call irreversibly realizes the strategy position, unwires yieldStrategy, freezes emissions and latches PoolState.Migrating. An owner reasonably expects a one-way door to pre-flight the preconditions its own documentation calls mandatory. (2) An owner expects a constructor to reject a nonsensical configuration. The surprise is not 'I typed the same address twice' -- that part is a plain typo. The surprise is that an unrejected constructor typo becomes an IRREVERSIBLE freeze of a funded pool that no admin action can undo. Surprise => footgun => in scope at honest severity.

classification.assetImpact: No value is lost or stolen in any leg. Users always retain the permissionless userMigrate exit (proven working even with the migrator pointed at a dead address), and on a healthy source R == P so the snapshot credit is full principal. The impact is availability of a live instance with three funded pools.
attackPath: 1. Owner deploys CrossVersionMigrator with a destination that is unwired, wrong, or -- in the severity-carrying leg -- the SAME address as oldStaker. The constructor accepts it: only zero-address checks exist.

2. Owner calls initiateMigration(token). It forwards unconditionally. The old pool's strategy is realized, the strategy is unwired, the (R,P) snapshot is taken, emissions freeze and PoolState latches to Migrating. This is irreversible: the pool cannot return to Active except through finalizeAndReset, which requires the staker set to be EMPTY.

3. ALIASING LEG: every subsequent migrate() reverts forever, because depositFor requires PoolState.Active and the destination pool is the very pool just frozen. There is no owner action that unwinds this -- no un-migrate, no retarget (both ends immutable by design, section (B)), and finalizeAndReset is blocked while any staker remains.

4. The only route back to Active is EVERY user in the pool individually calling userMigrate, after which the owner may finalizeAndReset and re-stake the base from scratch. Any single inactive, lost-key or unresponsive staker wedges the pool in Migrating PERMANENTLY -- no emissions, no staking, no privileged clear.
classification.likelihood: low for the aliasing leg (it requires a specific and fairly gross deployment error), moderate for the ordinary destination-wiring legs. Note that C4 Medium does not require high likelihood -- it explicitly accommodates a path with stated assumptions and external requirements.
classification.assumptions: The owner is non-malicious throughout (Law 3). The severity-carrying leg assumes a same-address constructor argument; the low-severity legs assume an ordinary wiring omission.
classification.externalRequirements: A deployment/wiring error by a trusted, non-malicious owner. No adversary.
classification.severityScoping: REVISED 2026-08-27 (see severityReversal): there is no Medium-carrying leg. The aliasing leg -- previously believed to be remedy-less and therefore to carry a Medium -- is owner-recoverable via StableStaker.setMigrator (src/StableStaker.sol:200) in 3 transactions with no user cooperation, which puts it on the same footing as the ordinary wiring-order legs (unregistered token, unset migrator, ungranted minter rights, wrong immutable destination). ALL legs are Low. PRIOR TEXT, superseded: The Medium is carried SOLELY by the aliasing leg and, more generally, by the absence of any destination precondition check on an irreversible action. The ordinary wiring-order legs -- unregistered token, unset migrator, ungranted minter rights, wrong immutable destination -- are LOW on their own: migrate() reverts atomically, the migrator never holds tokens, and every missing leg is an ordinary owner call on the live destination or a migrator redeploy. Stating this split explicitly so the Medium label is not read as covering more than it does.

classifiedFindings.justification: REVISED 2026-08-27. C4 Low/QA. The deflation from Medium is accepted because the sole basis for the Medium -- an availability outcome with NO privileged remedy -- was empirically refuted: the owner can re-point StableStaker.migrator at a correctly-wired replacement (setMigrator, src/StableStaker.sol:200, ungated), so recovery is an ordinary 3-transaction owner operation, not a bank-run-style coordinated user exit. The finding is NOT withdrawn and is NOT downgraded to nothing: under Law 3 the consequence of omitting every destination precondition check on an irreversible action remains non-obvious to a competent non-malicious owner, so it stays a reportable footgun -- at Low, in the QA bundle, with its mitigations intact. It is emphatically NOT a malicious-owner vector. PRIOR TEXT, superseded: C4 Medium reads 'assets not at direct risk, but the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted'. That is exactly this finding's shape, and I decline both the inflation to High (no assets are ever lost or stealable -- userMigrate is permissionless, unpausable and pays full principal on a healthy source) and the deflation to QA. The deflation fails because the aliasing leg produces an availability outcome with NO privileged remedy: a funded pool latched into Migrating where recovery is not an owner call but a coordinated manual exit by the entire user base, and where a single unresponsive staker makes the freeze permanent. Calling that 'recoverable' is true only in the sense that a bank run is recoverable. Under Law 3 the consequence is non-obvious -- the NatSpec documents the wiring requirement without disclosing that its violation is undetectable until after the irreversible step, and says nothing about aliasing being constructible -- so this is a reportable owner footgun, not a suppressible obvious misconfiguration. It is emphatically NOT a malicious-owner vector and must not be written up as one.
classifiedFindings.recommendedMitigation: Two independent one-line guards. (1) In the constructor: require(address(_oldStaker) != address(_newStaker), "Migrator: same staker"). (2) In initiateMigration, before forwarding, assert the destination preconditions section (C) already declares mandatory -- that newStaker has the token registered and is in PoolState.Active, and that newStaker's migrator is address(this). Both are pure pre-flight checks and neither weakens the deliberate immutability of the two targets (section B).
classifiedFindings.poc: workspace/stable-staker/test/poc/PoC_CVM_WiringRecovery.t.sol (4/4, classifier-verified). test_same_staker_constructor_is_inert_but_still_burns_the_pool is the severity-carrying test; the other three bound the reach.
classifiedFindings.humanReviewReason: Genuine two-agent split under Law 3. My adjudication is recorded in full above so the owner can overturn it on the record rather than re-litigate it. If the owner considers a same-address constructor argument obvious enough to be trusted-owner territory, the residual -- the total absence of destination precondition checks on an irreversible action -- still stands at Low.

severityReversal.reversedBy: poc-validator (empirical refutation), independently confirmed by severity-auditor (source re-read); recorded by finding-manager
severityReversal.premiseThatFailed: The Medium rested ENTIRELY on the aliasing leg having NO privileged remedy -- see the superseded arbitration below, which states 'there is no owner action that unwinds this -- no un-migrate, no retarget (both ends immutable by design, section (B))'. That inference conflated two different pointers. The MIGRATOR's _oldStaker/_newStaker endpoints are indeed immutable, but the STAKER's `migrator` pointer is NOT: StableStaker.setMigrator (src/StableStaker.sol:200) is a plain `external onlyOwner` setter that writes `migrator = _migrator` and emits MigratorSet, with NO poolState gate, NO pause gate and NO exists gate. The owner therefore retains a full privileged remedy without touching the immutable migrator: deploy a correctly-wired replacement migrator and re-point the staker at it. Recovery is 3 owner transactions with ZERO user cooperation -- not 'a coordinated manual exit by the entire user base', and not 'permanent if a single staker is unresponsive'.
evidence: poc-validator: REFUTED the 'no owner remedy' premise empirically. workspace/stable-staker/test/poc/PoC_CVM_WiringRecovery.t.sol re-run 4/4 from a clean `forge clean` rebuild; the validator probe demonstrated the owner-side re-point path that the arbitration asserted did not exist.

severity-auditor: INDEPENDENTLY verified the mechanism by reading src/StableStaker.sol:200 in source at 8856781 (not by trusting the validator's report) and ruled the downgrade CORRECT. No third reversal was proposed.
finding-manager: re-read src/StableStaker.sol:199-203 at 8856781 before persisting this record. setMigrator is ungated as described.

classifiedFindings.label: L-01
classifiedFindings.title: CrossVersionMigrator's batch-survival guard tests the SOURCE credit while the revert fires on the DESTINATION credit (dust poison)

arbitration.questionPut: Does layer (ii) -- a wedge no privileged actor can clear -- meet the C4 Medium availability test?
arbitration.answer: NO. Low is confirmed. Reasoning below; I considered Medium seriously and set out exactly why it fails, so the decision is auditable rather than reflexive.
whyMediumFails: The asset whose availability is denied is the SOURCE pool's revival, and this is the CROSS-version migrator: its destination is by construction a DIFFERENT staker. The pool being wedged in Migrating is the one being retired. Blocking finalizeAndReset on a pool nobody intends to reuse is a materially smaller harm than the phrase 'the pool can never be revived' suggests.

No user is impaired. Every non-dust user migrates normally once the dust address is excluded from the batch. The wedge-holder is not trapped either: userMigrate is permissionless, unpausable, and pays them p_i*min(R,P)/P -- full value on a healthy source. Nobody's funds are delayed beyond a single re-batch.

Layer (i) degrades but does not deny. An operator facing Sybil-planted dust can eth_call/simulate the batch and bisect to identify the offending addresses; the work is bounded and off-chain, and each failed batch reverts atomically with the migrator holding nothing.

The Tier-3 stateful campaign NEVER reached this path -- cohort principals sit far above the wei band -- so the evidence base is the dedicated dust tests, not the invariant campaign. I am recording that honestly rather than borrowing the campaign's weight.
whatRaisesItWithinLow: The mitigating framing of 'accidental dust' UNDERSTATES it: PoC_CVM_DustPoison plants the position deliberately via stake-then-withdraw-to-1-wei, so this is a PERMISSIONLESS GRIEFING VECTOR costing an attacker only gas, not merely a rounding accident. A deliberate griefer has no incentive to self-exit, which is precisely what layer (ii) depends on.

NatSpec section (D) and story-018 both explicitly CLAIM this failure mode is closed by the `if (amounts[i] > 0)` guard, and (D) goes further by naming off-chain pre-filtering -- the actual remedy -- 'a landmine' that was REJECTED. An operator has therefore been told, in the contract's own documentation, that the thing that can happen cannot happen, and told not to use the workaround that works. Per project law a falsely-exhaustive doc raises severity; here it lifts this from a rounding note to a solid, high-band Low and makes it a Law-2 faithfulness defect that must appear in spec-conformance, never in the gas/QA noise bundle.

classification.assetImpact: None. No value is lost, no credit is mis-booked; batches revert atomically and the migrator never custodies tokens.
attackPath: 1. Attacker (or an ordinary user, by accident) stakes and withdraws down to a 1-wei residual position on the source pool. Cost: gas.
2. Owner calls initiateMigration, then migrate() on a batch containing that address.
3. batchMigrate returns amounts[i] == 1, so the `if (amounts[i] > 0)` guard does NOT skip them -- the guard reads the SOURCE credit.

4. depositFor on the strategy-backed DESTINATION books credited == 0 for 1 wei (ERC4626 shares round down at an above-par share price) and trips require(credited > 0, "StableStaker: nothing credited"). The whole batch reverts atomically, taking every honest user in it down.

5. Layer (ii): that address can never be batch-migrated -- CrossVersionMigrator exposes no raw passthrough and StableStaker.batchMigrate is onlyMigrator -- and finalizeAndReset requires an empty staker set, so the retiring pool stays Migrating until the holder voluntarily calls userMigrate.
classification.likelihood: the accidental window is tiny and closed-form (ceil(sharePrice)-1 wei above par, 1 wei below par, 0 at par or against an idle destination; <=9 wei across 2000 fuzz runs). The DELIBERATE window is not rare at all -- an attacker simply constructs a position inside it.
classification.assumptions: The destination is strategy-backed at an above-par share price, which is the realistic production wiring.
classification.externalRequirements: None beyond gas for the griefing variant.

classifiedFindings.justification: C4 Low covers state handling and spec deviation, and that is what this is: a guard that reads the wrong quantity, plus a documentation block that certifies the resulting failure mode as impossible. It does not reach Medium because neither prong of the Medium definition is satisfied -- there is no value leak of any size, and the availability denial lands on the revival of a pool that the migration is retiring, while every user including the wedge-holder retains a permissionless, full-value exit. Elevating it would be the overstatement this pipeline rejects. Equally, it is not informational: the false safety claim in NatSpec (D) actively misdirects the operator away from the only workaround that functions, and the dust position is plantable on purpose for the price of gas, so it belongs in the report as a Low with the faithfulness defect routed to spec-conformance.
classifiedFindings.faithfulnessRouting: F-06 in spec-conformance.md. NatSpec section (D) and story-018 both assert batch survival that the implementation does not deliver.
classifiedFindings.recommendedMitigation: Move the guard to the quantity the revert actually reads: either have depositFor return the credited amount and skip on a zero destination credit, or pre-simulate the destination credit in the loop. Failing that, correct section (D) to state plainly that the guard covers only a zero SOURCE credit and that a non-zero source credit rounding to zero on the destination still reverts the batch.
classifiedFindings.ledgerDisclosureNote: Same root-cause CLASS as open Lows bda951d9f1 (InPlaceMigrator.migrateIn) and bf5018deab (InPlaceMigrator._reinjectWithTopup), reborn on a NEW contract and therefore minting a fingerprint dedup cannot catch. Disclosed, not silently merged and not silently re-minted. What is genuinely new: neither sibling ships a guard for this failure; this contract does, and it reads the wrong quantity, so it carries a false safety claim the siblings do not. Fixing either sibling does not fix this, and vice versa.

classifiedFindings.label: L-02
classifiedFindings.title: NatSpec (E) and story-018 mis-attribute the uncompensated haircut to an underwater SOURCE; the destination-side haircut is independent and bites on a healthy migration

classification.assetImpact: Latent value leak on the destination credit leg: credited_i = credit_i * (MAX_BPS - slippageToleranceBps) / MAX_BPS. At 100 bps a cohort is booked 1% below its snapshot credit even at R == P; on $10M migrated that is $100k not credited to users.
attackPath: 1. Operator reads section (E) -- 'This contract redeposits exactly what it received and no more' -- and story-018, both of which scope the shortfall to an underwater SOURCE.
2. Operator concludes a healthy source implies no user loss, and proceeds without checking the destination's slippage tolerance.
3. The destination is wired to a market/AMM-backed strategy; the haircut applies in full on a perfectly healthy migration.
classification.likelihood: low today -- ZERO reach on the currently-targeted direct ERC4626YieldStrategy route (~1 wei share-rounding only). The exposure is latent and contingent on wiring a market/AMM-backed destination.
classification.assumptions: A haircutting destination strategy is wired at some future point.

classifiedFindings.justification: Low, on the documentation axis only. The Medium value-leak prong is not reached because the reach against the actually-wired destination is ~1 wei of share rounding; the dollar figure above is a latent, contingent exposure, and pricing an unwired configuration at Medium would be speculation on future code. What is real and reportable today is the Law-3 footgun: section (E) reads as EXHAUSTIVE, and story-018's test plan repeats the conflation by describing MockYieldStrategy.setDepositSlippageBps as 'how underwater conditions are simulated', so the healthy-source-plus-haircutting-destination case is unmodeled by both the story and the test suite. A competent non-malicious owner would be surprised, and a falsely-exhaustive doc raises rather than sanitizes.
classifiedFindings.scopeDecision: SPLIT upheld. The DOCUMENTATION defect is filed here as new. The CODE defect (the credit asymmetry itself) is NOT a new finding -- it is open Low 4f143a9573, same root cause, unchanged severity and reach in kind; scope-extend that entry rather than minting a second fingerprint for the same asymmetry. Note for the writer: 3d61c9552f and b5218ab2 sit on the DELETED migrateOut path and are the WRONG repoint target.

classifiedFindings.label: L-03
classifiedFindings.title: Golden-rule CI gate and PreToolUse hook both fail to prevent DELETION of src/versions/IStableStakerV1.sol

classification.assetImpact: None directly. The perpetual-snapshot ritual that stories 014/015/018 rely on is unenforced, so the golden-rule triad's frozen record can be removed with no gate tripping.
attackPath: 1. The snapshot file is deleted (refactor, bad merge, or an agent edit).
2. tools/check-migration-surface.sh:52-56 prints 'no version snapshots yet' on an empty set WITHOUT setting a failure status, so CI stays green.
3. The PreToolUse hook counts `function <name>(` occurrences; IStableStakerV1 INHERITS rather than declares the triad, so deletion changes the count by exactly zero and the hook does not fire.
classification.likelihood: moderate over time; no adversary required.

classifiedFindings.justification: Low. This is process/tooling rather than on-chain state, so no C4 Medium prong is engaged -- no protocol function or availability is affected at runtime and no value is at risk. It is nonetheless a genuine Law-2 faithfulness defect backed by an empirically tested 6-mutation table, and it compounds CLASS-008: a snapshot whose self-description is inaccurate AND whose deletion is unguarded is weaker than either defect implies alone.

classifiedFindings.label: L-04
classifiedFindings.title: story-015's snapshot-extraction ritual targets master HEAD rather than the deploy commit; its drift premise is already materially false

classification.assetImpact: None. The snapshot does not describe the deployed contract it purports to freeze: STAKER_VERSION is an ABI member of the extracted snapshot that the LIVE deployed instance lacks.
attackPath: 1. The ritual extracts from master HEAD rather than the deploy commit.
2. The resulting snapshot drifts from the deployed ABI; it is accurate member-by-member today, but the PROCEDURE is not repeatable and its own premise is already false.
classification.likelihood: certain -- already materially false at HEAD.

classifiedFindings.justification: Low. A spec/process deviation with no runtime asset or availability consequence, which is squarely the C4 QA/Low band. It matters because CrossVersionMigrator's whole design rationale (section A, the narrowest-possible-dependency argument) rests on the golden-rule snapshot being a faithful record of the deployed surface, and the extraction procedure does not produce one.

classifiedFindings.label: L-05
classifiedFindings.title: CrossVersionMigrator has no rescue/sweep path while sibling InPlaceMigrator does, and the NatSpec never records the omission as a decision

classification.assetImpact: Any token reaching the migrator outside the migrate() flow is permanently unrecoverable. The deposit loop pulls exactly amounts[i] and never a surplus.
attackPath: 1. An owner PRE-FUNDS the migrator intending to cover the haircut -- which section (E)'s wording arguably invites (see CLASS-004).
2. migrate() consumes only amounts[i]; the surplus stays in the migrator.
3. No rescue function exists, so the surplus is lost permanently.
classification.likelihood: low. Nothing can arrive via migrate(): Tier-3 invariant_01_migratorTokenConservation proved a per-call balance delta of exactly zero across 750k Foundry calls and 1.0M Medusa calls. Exposure is donation, rebase, or misdirected transfer only.
classification.assumptions: Funds reach the migrator by a route other than migrate().
classification.externalRequirements: An owner pre-funding action, a rebasing token, or a misdirected transfer.

classifiedFindings.justification: Low. The loss is real and permanent but the reach is bounded to funds that should never be there, and the Tier-3 conservation proof rules out the normal flow entirely, so no protocol function or availability is impacted and there is no path an attacker profits from. It stays above informational for the Law-3 reason that the omission is an UNDOCUMENTED asymmetry with a sibling contract that does ship a rescue path -- an owner reasoning by analogy from InPlaceMigrator would be surprised -- and because CLASS-004's documentation defect creates precisely the pre-funding scenario this missing path fails to remedy. The two findings should cite each other.

classifiedFindings.label: Q-01
classifiedFindings.title: IStableStakerV1.sol NatSpec inaccuracies: the '16 events' claim and the 'Known external coupling' block are both incomplete

attackPath: Not applicable -- documentation accuracy only.

classifiedFindings.justification: QA/informational. (a) 'the 16 events emitted by the deployed V1 contract' omits OwnershipTransferred, Paused, Unpaused and the OZ custom-error set. (b) The 'Known external coupling' block omits IStableStakerMigratable, which the frozen file itself inherits. Genuinely informational standalone -- no state, value or availability consequence. Recorded rather than dropped because a falsely-exhaustive doc block carries no suppression authority and because it compounds CLASS-005: the snapshot's self-description is wrong AND its deletion is unguarded.

classifiedFindings.label: Q-02
classifiedFindings.title: migrate's two loops iterate different bounds (amounts.length vs users.length)

attackPath: 1. A future staker version returns a shorter amounts array than users.length.
2. Line 122 sums over amounts.length while line 133 iterates users.length and indexes amounts[i], yielding an out-of-bounds panic rather than a clean revert.
classification.likelihood: nil today -- both targets are immutable and owner-chosen, and the trusted oldStaker returns a same-length array.
classification.assumptions: A future staker redesign returns a differently-sized array.
classification.externalRequirements: A future staker version, i.e. speculation on code that does not exist.

classifiedFindings.justification: QA. Not exploitable and it depends on future code, which is explicitly a discouraged basis for severity. It is filed rather than dropped because it is a Law-2 nick rather than pure style: it directly contradicts section (A)'s stated goal of surviving arbitrary future staker redesigns, which is the contract's central design claim. Recall beats report-tidiness.
classifiedFindings.recallNote: Absent from the supplied candidate inventory; filed under the no-silent-drop rule.

classifiedFindings.label: Q-03
classifiedFindings.title: CLAUDE.md's description of golden-rule enforcement layer 1 over-states what the layer actually does

attackPath: Not applicable -- documentation accuracy only.

classifiedFindings.justification: QA. The compile-time bypass named by story-014's review IS genuinely closed -- that half is faithful and is credited as such. The residual is that the CLAUDE.md prose claims more coverage than the layer delivers, which compounds CLASS-005's demonstration that the deletion axis is entirely unguarded. No runtime consequence, hence QA rather than Low.
classifiedFindings.recallNote: Absent from the supplied candidate inventory; filed under the no-silent-drop rule.
classifiedFindings.noteOnF04: F-04 (story-018's 'strict functional superset' claim) was verified TRUE and correctly yields NO finding. Recorded so its absence is explicit rather than silent.

correctedAnnotations.rationale: The classifier dismissed the code-scanner's QA proposal on the ground that 'recoverability is not the Law-3 test' and that the scanner's own fourth test documented a leg 'where the owner has NO remedy at all'. Both halves fail. The scanner's recoverability argument was not merely a mitigation argument -- it correctly bounded the IMPACT, which is precisely what sets the C4 severity band once Law-3 reportability is established. And the 'no remedy at all' reading of test_same_staker_constructor_is_inert_but_still_burns_the_pool was wrong on the facts: the owner remedy runs through StableStaker.setMigrator (src/StableStaker.sol:200), which the arbitration never considered because it reasoned only about the migrator's own immutable endpoints. The code-scanner reached the correct band (QA/Low) by correct reasoning; recording it as UNDERSTATING inverted the calibration signal and would have taught the wrong lesson to a future run.
